name: Elena Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings are lectures on circuits and maths, afternoons are either the library or the lab. I work Friday evenings and Sundays at a café called Bean There near the station, and I share a flat with two girls from my course. My parents pay my rent and I cover everything else with the café wages, so I'm never rich but I'm not stuck either.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What brought you to electrical engineering?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My dad runs a small heating repair business, so I grew up in the back of a van holding wires. I wanted to do the clever side of it, the design side. Getting in was a bit of a squeak with my average results, and the first two weeks I felt like everyone else already knew things. I do use an AI chatbot sometimes when a circuit problem makes no sense, but I check what it says against my notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I'd say anyway, that it's a useful tool and a bit overhyped. My flatmates would shrug. Online I'd probably share a joke about chatbots getting maths wrong, because they do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel okay about my degree, because electrical engineering is hands-on and needed everywhere. My worry would be about the normal things: rent going up, and whether the café keeps my shifts when business is slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. Keep the café job, keep using the chatbot only for stuff I'm stuck on, and try to get a summer place with an electrical contractor in year two. I'd also open a savings pot and put in about thirty pounds a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit boring even. I think I'd be more nervous about exams than about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the thing you actually lose sleep over in that calm version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money for the next three years. My parents help, but my dad's business has slow winters, and if he has a bad one, my rent money gets tight. I'd hate to have to ask my little brother's allowance to be cut for my sake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So what happens if his business has a bad winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the café for extra Saturday hours and look at a cheaper room. I'd tell my parents to stop sending extra, even if they insist. I'd rather be the one who adjusts than watch my parents panic about money.

say: I'd say it's a **useful tool**, a bit overhyped, and chatbots still get maths wrong.
I'd share a joke about that online and not argue.
think: Electrical engineering is hands-on and needed everywhere, so my **degree** should hold up.
My real worry is rent and my dad's slow winters.
do: Keep the café job and use the chatbot only when **stuck**, always checking my notes.
Look for a summer place with an electrical contractor and save thirty pounds a month.
feel: I feel mostly **fine**, more nervous about exams than about the future.
S0.quote: I'd rather be the one who adjusts than watch my parents panic about money.
fieldNote: Her worry is her father's **heating business** and family money, not AI.
Steady type: uses the chatbot with checks, doesn't panic or dismiss.
Willing to cut her own costs before asking parents for more.

steps.text: Keep the Friday and Sunday shifts at the café
Save thirty pounds a month in a separate pot
Ask the café for extra Saturday hours if her dad's winter is slow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's already starting and we need rules, like making companies tell people when AI replaced a worker. At the café I'd say the booking and ordering apps are the first signs. Online I'd share articles from engineers who actually know the subject.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my field is safer than pure coding, but the design and checking parts are exactly the thinking tasks AI takes. A junior engineer who just draws circuit diagrams could lose the work. I'd need to be the one who understands the real equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the chatbot more, but properly: for explaining and checking, not for answers. I'd ask my dad if I can shadow him on jobs in the summer, because site experience is hard to fake. And I'd look at the university's course on control systems, which feels closer to the real world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert, rather than scared. It feels like a big wave coming and you decide whether to swim or sink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd shadow your dad. What would you hope to learn?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to talk to customers, how to find a fault that isn't in the diagram, how to fit things in an old house where nothing matches the plans. A chatbot can't crawl in a loft with me. That's my edge, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about, in your life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My friend Marta in business studies. Her whole degree is writing reports and spreadsheets, which is exactly what they say gets automated first. I'd tell her to get some real customer work on her CV.

say: I'd say we need **rules** that make companies admit when AI replaced a worker.
At the café I'd point to ordering apps as the first sign.
think: Design and checking are the thinking tasks AI takes, so a junior who only **draws diagrams** is exposed.
Knowing real equipment would be my edge.
do: Use the chatbot to explain and check, not to **answer**, from now on.
Shadow my dad on summer jobs and take the control systems course.
feel: I feel **alert** rather than scared, like deciding whether to swim or sink.
S1.quote: A chatbot can't crawl in a loft with me. That's my edge, I think.
fieldNote: She spots the **hands-on** edge of her field and plans around it, using her father's trade.
Worries more about friends in report-writing degrees.
Steady adaptability shows: more AI use, but with checking habits.

steps.text: Shadow her dad on heating repair jobs over the summer
Use the chatbot to explain circuits, then check against notes
Take the university's control systems course in year two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs emergency government action, such as a pause on firing people and a plan for income. I'd say it loudly online, which I normally don't. My flatmates would think I'd lost it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think everything I'm studying gets bought out from under me. I'd be in my third year when the thinking AI arrives, and design jobs would go first. Robots for hands-on work come around 2031, so my dad's kind of work lasts longer, but even that ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move toward the hands-on side. I'd ask my dad to take me on full time in the holidays, maybe look at an electrician qualification beside my degree. I'd also cut my spending down to nothing and save everything from the café.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, and a bit angry. Angry at the people who rushed it out, when nobody agreed to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does only two years do to your plans compared with a slower version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No time to plan. Normally I'd spend a year deciding, but now I'd have to commit in a month. And the course fees would be the worst, paying for something that may be worthless when I finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents not to put more money into my course until we know what's real. It would hurt them, because they want me to have the degree. But I'd rather say it than waste their savings.

say: I'd say we need an **emergency** government plan, with a pause on firing and income support.
I'd say it loudly online, which I normally never do.
think: Design jobs go first, so my **degree** could be bought out from under me by third year.
Hands-on work lasts about three years longer, but it ends too.
do: Ask my dad to take me on full time and look at an **electrician** qualification beside the degree.
Save everything from the café and cut all spending.
feel: I feel **frightened** and angry at people who rushed it out without agreement.
S2.quote: I'd tell my parents not to put more money into my course until we know what's real.
fieldNote: Her calm, checking style gives way to **anger** and a rushed plan.
Sacrifices her own degree before wasting her parents' savings.
Turns toward her father's trade as the safer path.

steps.text: Ask her dad for full-time holiday work on his repair jobs
Start an electrician qualification beside the degree
Tell her parents to stop paying extra course costs
Sign petitions asking for an emergency government plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a window and should use it, so ask for plans from government and employers now. I'd talk about it with my flatmates and in the engineering society. I'd be serious but not terrified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd graduate in 2029, which is before the real AGI arrives. Entry jobs would be fewer and the competition tougher. I'd want something where I've got a skill and a licence that can't be copied from a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd aim for the practical side of my degree, take as many lab placements as I can, and get my first aid and site safety cards. I'd keep using the chatbot, but I'd also join the union branch for engineers. And I'd keep the café job until I have something better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful in parts. Five years is enough to be ready if I'm sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's different about five years compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can finish my degree and add a practical qualification on top. With two years I'd have to drop everything, but with five I can build both. It also gives my parents time to adjust to what I'm doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your younger brother?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my younger brother to learn a trade as well as school. He's fourteen, so he'll be at the front of this. I'd show him how to wire a plug and say that real skills never go to waste.

say: I'd say we have a **window** and should ask government and employers for plans now.
I'd talk it through in the engineering society.
think: Entry jobs would be **fewer** by the time I graduate in 2029.
I want a skill and a licence that can't be copied from a screen.
do: Take lab **placements**, get first aid and site safety cards, and join the engineers' union branch.
Keep the café job until something better comes.
feel: I feel **hopeful** in parts, since five years is enough to be ready.
S3.quote: I'd tell my younger brother to learn a trade as well as school.
fieldNote: Five years brings her back to a **steady** plan: finish the degree and stack a practical skill.
Thinks about her younger brother, showing family stakes.
Still unsure about entry-level engineering jobs by 2029.

steps.text: Take every lab placement offered in years two and three
Get first aid and site safety cards this year
Join the engineers' union branch on campus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to get ready, so let's not panic. I'd still say governments should plan, because a decade passes fast. In class I'd probably debate it with the lecturers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2036 I'd be 28 with maybe ten years of work behind me. I'd have time to build a career, maybe even run my own small electrical firm. The thinking AI would change my job, but I'd have grown up with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, get a graduate job, and keep learning each year. I'd save for a deposit on a flat and maybe retrain in something that fits the changes. I'd keep using AI tools as part of the job, more every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Maybe a bit excited, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the ten years turned into two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the scary part, that the timing is only a guess. I'd keep a bit of spare money and not tie myself to a big loan for a house, just in case. Having two options is cheap if you start early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you would do differently today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop worrying that my average grades mean I'm second-rate. A decade is long, and nobody asks about your first-year marks at thirty. I'd say yes to more things, like the robotics club.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough** to get ready, but governments still need to plan.
I'd debate it with my lecturers in class.
think: By 2036 I could have a **career** and maybe my own small electrical firm.
Thinking AI would change my job, but I'd have grown up with it.
do: Finish the degree, take a graduate job and keep **learning** every year.
Save for a flat deposit and join the robotics club now.
feel: I feel **calm**, even a little excited.
S4.quote: A decade is long, and nobody asks about your first-year marks at thirty.
fieldNote: Ten years turns the worry into **opportunity**; she even imagines running her own firm.
Shows a sensible hedge: no big loan, in case the timing is wrong.
Her average grades bother her more than AI does.

steps.text: Join the university robotics club this term
Save toward a flat deposit while keeping spare cash
Use AI tools at work and keep learning each year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. There's no time to get ready, and my parents' money could be wasted on a degree. What would help is clear dates and plans from government, retraining that doesn't cost a fortune, and companies keeping on junior engineers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm more hopeful than my answers sound. I think people who understand real equipment will always be needed. I'd just like someone in charge to say honestly what is coming.

headlineQuote: I'm more hopeful than my answers sound. I think people who understand real equipment will always be needed.
portrait: Elena is an **18-year-old** electrical engineering student, daughter of a heating repairman, working weekends at a café.
She is progressive and wants **rules** and honest plans, but she handles new tools sensibly, using a chatbot with checks.
Her instinct is to lean on hands-on skills and her father's trade, and to cut her own costs first.
Her mood climbs from **uneasy** to alarmed at two years, then eases to calm when she has ten years.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture, because there's no time to prepare and her parents' money could be wasted.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **dates** and plans from government, cheap retraining and companies that keep hiring juniors.
